paragraphs.text: A loose [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Yunnan, left unpressed after fermenting. Its leaf was wetted and heaped in a [damp pile](shou:wet-piling), where microbes make their own heat. The pile is covered to hold that heat in, turned about once a week to spread it and let air in, and kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf begins to char. After one to two months the leaf is dried.

The pile does in weeks what raw pu’er takes years of keeping to do, so a ripe tea is ready to drink soon after it is made. Yunnan [learned the method](shou:piling-1973) in 1973, when a team of seven from the Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan factories went to study it at the Guangzhou tea factory.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
